events.event: ABHI Microfinance Bank raised over Rs. 2 billion through the book-building portion of its IPO on the Pakistan Stock Exchange.
events.source_excerpt:
ABHI Microfinance Bank has raised about Rs. 2.05 billion through the book-building portion of its IPO, after demand ran past the shares on offer, according to Pakistan Stock Exchange book-building data and a company announcement.
The book-building tranche covered 99 million of the bank’s 132 million ordinary shares on offer, at a floor price of Rs. 15.00.
PSX data show an indicative strike price of Rs. 15.50, with bids for about 157.17 million shares, which is roughly 159 percent of the offer at the floor and about 106% at the strike.
The company said the book build is Pakistan’s first fintech-led microfinance bank IPO. It reported bids of more than Rs. 2.4 billion, with strong interest from foreign funds, local institutions, and high-net-worth investors.
The remaining 33 million shares will go to the public at the strike price on November 12 and 13, 2026.
ABHI had earlier said the full IPO could raise between Rs. 2 billion and Rs. 3 billion, with proceeds meant to expand its loan book and strengthen its capital base. ProPakistani covered that plan in an earlier report.

Trump made the change public in a statement on his Truth Social platform, writing that Miller would take over from Susie Wiles on Monday—less than a week after Republicans lost the House and Senate in a searing rebuke of Trump’s policy agenda.
In recent days, Trump has privately blamed Wiles for the worst Republican midterm performance in decades, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday, the sources say.
Trump broadly considered three candidates to replace Wiles, the sources say: special envoy Steve Witkoff, director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, and Miller.

events.event: The Sindh government officially declared Tharparkar a calamity-hit district and ordered emergency measures due to severe drought conditions.
events.source_excerpt:
Published November 07, 2026
KARACHI: The Sindh government has decided to officially declare Tharparkar a calamity-hit district amid drought-like conditions across the region.
The decision was taken during a meeting chaired by Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah, who also directed the authorities to take immediate measures to address the situation in Tharparkar.
The briefing informed the chief minister that all seven talukas of Tharparkar were facing drought-like conditions, with between 85% and 90% of crops either destroyed or rendered unproductive.
According to the briefing, the agriculture extension department estimated crop losses at around 90%, while uneven rainfall had caused crops and natural grass to dry up before reaching maturity.
The chief minister was told that rainfall recorded across Tharparkar's seven talukas in September 2026 ranged from just one millimetre to 36 millimetres.
CM Murad directed the authorities to ensure the provision of drinking water to the people of Tharparkar and ordered the immediate repair and restoration of inactive reverse osmosis plants.
He also directed that all existing sources of water supply be restored without delay.
The chief minister instructed the chief secretary to examine the feasibility of laying a water pipeline from Naukot to Mithi and undertake long-term planning for water supply to the area.
He further sought recommendations on measures that could be taken to support livestock affected by the drought.
CM Murad directed continuous monitoring of relief measures in drought-affected areas, saying the Sindh government would not leave the affected people of Tharparkar alone and would provide every possible assistance.

events.event: Pakistani oil refineries face negative refining margins as international petrol prices fell below crude oil prices.
events.source_excerpt:
Pakistan’s oil refineries are facing fresh financial pressure as international petrol prices have fallen below crude oil prices, pushing refining margins into negative territory for the first time in recent history.
According to Topline Research, petrol refining margins dropped to negative $1 per barrel on a seven-day rolling average basis as of November 6. International petrol prices stood at $105.90 per barrel, compared with Dubai crude oil at $106.90 per barrel. On November 5, the daily refining margin fell further to negative $5 per barrel.
The decline became visible in international price data compiled by OGRA and Topline Research. Petrol and Dubai crude prices moved relatively closely throughout much of October before falling sharply towards the end of the month. By November 5, petrol prices had dropped below crude oil prices, putting additional pressure on refinery profitability.
Refining margins, also known as cracks, represent the difference between the selling price of refined petroleum products and the cost of crude oil used to produce them. When petrol prices fall below crude oil prices, refiners face losses on petrol production.
The situation has become more challenging for domestic refineries following the imposition of a Rs. 49 per litre levy on petrol. The combination of negative international refining margins and the additional domestic levy is expected to further squeeze the profitability of Pakistan’s refining sector.
The latest development adds to the financial challenges facing local refineries as international fuel prices and domestic levies continue to affect their operating margins.

The price of a household liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) cylinder in Pakistan has surged to an all-time high of Rs. 6,498, up nearly 80 percent since the beginning of 2026.
According to the latest available data as of November 5, the price of an 11.67kg cylinder has climbed sharply. This has added extra pressure on households that rely on LPG for cooking and heating.
The situation has been particularly difficult for households without access to piped natural gas, as well as those facing irregular gas supplies.
Pakistan has also faced disruptions in LPG imports following the closure of key border crossings with Iran in October. Iran accounts for a significant share of Pakistan’s LPG imports, and the disruption has tightened supplies in the domestic market.
LPG has recently been selling for as much as Rs. 500 per kg in Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, while prices in some hilly areas have reached Rs. 600 per kg.
The difference between official and market prices has also become a big problem.
The Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) set the official LPG price for November at Rs. 294.07 per kilogram, putting the notified price of an 11.8kg domestic cylinder at Rs. 3,470.09. However, consumers have been paying double in the retail market.
With winter approaching, higher demand for cooking and heating fuel could add further pressure on LPG supplies and household budgets.

events.event: The International Energy Agency reported that global oil supply exceeded demand in the fourth quarter for the first time since the war in Iran began.
events.source_excerpt:
Published November 13, 2026
Global oil supplies are expected to exceed demand in the fourth quarter, after increased Gulf exports led to a market surplus in October for the first time since the Iran war, the International Energy Agency said Friday.
Even though attacks on tankers trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz have continued, Gulf shipments reached 18.4 million barrels per day (mb/d) -- though that was still 26% below pre-war levels, the Paris-based agency said in its monthly report.
"The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the IEA said.
Prices have fallen sharply in recent weeks as more vessels prove willing to make the risky transit through the Strait of Hormuz under US escort.
Iran effectively closed the crucial strait in the early months of the war launched by the United States and Israel in late February.
That helped overall oil supply to rise by three million barrels per day in September and a further 2.3 million barrels in October, the IEA said.
But global demand is set to fall by 2.7 mb/d overall this year as oil prices remain well above pre-war levels and "accelerate electrification and fuel efficiencies across the global car fleet".
Diesel prices in particular stood at $180 per barrel in October, around 77% higher than before the war, as Iran struck refineries in neighbouring Gulf countries accused of aiding US attacks.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and other energy installations are also disrupting diesel supplies to the global market.
"The severe tightness in product supply, especially for diesel, remains the overriding concern of the broader market and consumers," the IEA said.

Since war erupted with the United States in February, Tehran has insisted that vessels obtain its authorisation to cross the strait and has attacked ships that do not comply.

NADRA shares steps to recover existing Pak ID accounts online
- By Kumail Shah -
- Nov 14, 2026
The National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) has shared steps for citizens to recover their Pak ID accounts if their CNIC numbers are already registered in the mobile app.
NADRA says that if users see an error saying their CNIC number is already linked to another account when registering on the Pak ID app, they should recover their existing account instead of making a new one.
To access their account, users should open the Pak ID app, enter their CNIC number on the login screen, and select the “Forgot Password” option. After that, they should enter their registered email address to receive a two-factor authentication (2FA) code.
Once users enter the verification code, they need to complete biometric verification to confirm their identity. After finishing these steps, they can access their Pak ID account.
The Pak ID app lets users access NADRA services like CNIC renewal, modification, replacement, and other identity-related applications. If citizens still have trouble logging in or registering, they can call NADRA’s helpline at 1777 for help.

Google One provides additional cloud storage that can be used across Google Drive, Gmail, and Google Photos. For users who regularly back up their photos, store documents online, or receive large email attachments, a paid storage subscription can be an important part of their digital routine.

events.event: Pakistan's domestic debt declined by Rs 1.636 trillion during the first quarter of FY27 to stand at Rs 57.757 trillion.
events.source_excerpt:
Pakistan’s domestic debt declined by Rs. 1.636 trillion during the first quarter of FY27, bringing the total outstanding debt to Rs. 57.757 trillion by the end of September 2026.
According to State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) data, domestic debt stood at Rs. 59.393 trillion on June 30, marking a significant reduction in government borrowing during July-September.
The government also stepped up debt repayments, with net retirement of scheduled bank debt reaching Rs. 1.847 trillion during July-October FY27, compared with Rs. 45 billion in the same period last year. Borrowing through Pakistan Investment Bonds (PIBs) declined by Rs. 1.756 trillion to Rs. 33.543 trillion, while Treasury bill borrowing fell by Rs. 1.163 trillion to Rs. 9.640 trillion.
The decline comes amid higher government revenues and fiscal consolidation efforts under Pakistan’s International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal recently said the fiscal deficit narrowed to 2.6% of GDP in FY26, compared with 5.4% in FY25.
Despite the quarterly decline, domestic debt increased by Rs. 4.331 trillion over the 12 months ending September 2026. Meanwhile, external debt rose by Rs. 700 billion in rupee terms, reaching Rs. 24.9 trillion by the end of September.

events.event: A technical glitch disrupted a US press conference addressing nationwide flight disruptions caused by aging technology.
events.source_excerpt:
Trump administration officials were left red-faced on Saturday when their public effort to address the massive tech disruption that grounded thousands of US flights was itself hit with embarrassing technical glitches.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy took the podium and began addressing a much-anticipated and televised press conference a day after a disastrous nationwide ground stop across US airspace — one blamed on ageing technology — when a deep, echoing hum began to emanate from the microphones and speakers.
“Check one two, three four, five six seven?” Duffy said into the mic.
As cameras rolled, he paused, looked around, and stepped away.
“[I] apologise for that,” he said, as technicians scrambled to replace microphones and adjust cables.
Duffy soon resumed, but brittle feedback hit the room seconds later and his demeanour shifted, presumably all-too-aware that the symbolism of an on-camera tech meltdown after such a major flight disruption was not going unnoticed.
“This is not operational? OK,” said Duffy, appearing deeply irritated.
“This is our kind of, uh, day.”
Duffy was speaking to reporters with the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, Bryan Bedford, and, ironically, with the FAA’s chief technology officer Rebecca Guy, who he said was doing a press conference with him for the first time.
Duffy and Bedford repeatedly pointed to ongoing systemic issues with transitioning from ageing air traffic control technology from the 1970s and 1980s to more modern equipment.
As technicians scrambled, US networks carried the awkward pause — lasting an excruciating three minutes — live on the air.
